approachQuestion.prompt:
Is the preparation order forced? A directed dependency graph is promised acyclic. Every vertex is a distinct job, and u->v means u must precede v. Return true exactly when there is only one valid ordering of all V jobs; return false when there are at least two. Disconnected jobs must also appear in the ordering.

Input: read-only outgoing adjacency lists, IDs 0..V-1; 1 <= V <= 200000, 0 <= E <= 400000, no duplicates or self-loops. The acyclic promise is reliable; no order needs to be returned.

Example 1: lists=[[1],[2],[]], output=true.
Example 2: lists=[[2],[2],[]], output=false: either 0 or 1 can be first.
Example 3: lists=[[],[]], output=false.

options.text: Use indegree elimination. Before each removal, require exactly one currently zero-indegree remaining job. If two or more are available, return false; otherwise remove the sole job and update neighbors. Return true after all jobs are removed.
options.feedback: Two available jobs have no unfinished prerequisite ordering them relative to each other, so either can be next and both choices extend to complete orders in a DAG. A sole choice at every step forces the entire sequence.

options.text: Return true because the graph is acyclic.
options.feedback: Acyclicity guarantees existence, not uniqueness. Example 3 has two isolated jobs and both [0,1] and [1,0] are valid.

options.text: Return true exactly when the original graph has one zero-indegree vertex, without checking later steps.
options.feedback: For lists=[[1,2],[],[]], only 0 is initially available, but after 0 both 1 and 2 are available. The orders [0,1,2] and [0,2,1] differ.

options.text: Enumerate all topological orders by branching on available jobs and count them, returning true only if the final count is one.
options.feedback: This is logically correct if the count is kept exactly, but can enumerate factorially many orders for isolated jobs. A pair of simultaneous choices already proves nonuniqueness, so complete enumeration is explicitly unnecessary inefficiency.

feedback.reason: Uniqueness is a property of every available frontier during dependency removal, not merely the first choice or the absence of cycles.
details: Build indegrees and queue all zero-indegree jobs. Before each removal, compare tail-head, the number of queued jobs. If it exceeds one, return false. Otherwise remove the only job and decrement all outgoing neighbor indegrees, adding newly zero neighbors. The DAG promise ensures a nonempty remaining graph always has an available job. Return true after V removals.
Two available zero-indegree jobs can be swapped, producing two valid orders. Exactly one choice at every step forces the order under the DAG promise. Queue length is read directly, not rescanned.

“Use indegree elimination. Before each removal, require exactly one currently zero-indegree remaining job. If two or more are available, return false; otherwise remove the sole job and update neighbors. Return true after all jobs are removed.”: Two available jobs have no unfinished prerequisite ordering them relative to each other, so either can be next and both choices extend to complete orders in a DAG. A sole choice at every step forces the entire sequence.
“Return true because the graph is acyclic.”: Acyclicity guarantees existence, not uniqueness. Example 3 has two isolated jobs and both [0,1] and [1,0] are valid.

“Return true exactly when the original graph has one zero-indegree vertex, without checking later steps.”: For lists=[[1,2],[],[]], only 0 is initially available, but after 0 both 1 and 2 are available. The orders [0,1,2] and [0,2,1] differ.

“Enumerate all topological orders by branching on available jobs and count them, returning true only if the final count is one.”: This is logically correct if the count is kept exactly, but can enumerate factorially many orders for isolated jobs. A pair of simultaneous choices already proves nonuniqueness, so complete enumeration is explicitly unnecessary inefficiency.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze unique-available-job. V counts jobs and E dependencies. Initialize V indegrees and scan all edges before elimination. Use a preallocated V-slot queue with head/tail indices and constant-time indexing, arithmetic and queue operations. No order is returned: output is a scalar boolean. Exclude input and scalar output; include indegrees and queue. No hashing, recursion, copying, shifting or amortized growth. Consider a DAG with a unique order so the loop does not return early.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard worst-case bound for the specified implementation.

options.text: O(V + E) time, O(V) auxiliary space
O(V + E) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(V(V + E)) time, O(V) auxiliary space
O(V + E) time, O(V + E) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Indegree construction and one elimination pass account for all work.
details: The option “O(V + E) time, O(V) auxiliary space” is tight: indegree initialization/build costs O(V+E), each job is removed once, and every edge is decremented once. Indegrees and queue require O(V) auxiliary storage. The option “O(V + E) time, O(1) auxiliary space” omits them. The option “O(V(V + E)) time, O(V) auxiliary space” incorrectly repeats the graph traversal per choice. The option “O(V + E) time, O(V + E) auxiliary space” counts edge storage that remains part of the read-only input. Checking queue length is constant time and does not scan the frontier.
